old:
Above the current price demand is elastic: rivals ignore a price rise, so customers switch away and revenue falls. Below it demand is inelastic: rivals match a cut, so few customers arrive and revenue still falls — at worst a price war starts.

The kink makes MR discontinuous at Q, and MC can shift anywhere within the gap without changing the profit-maximising price — so prices stay "sticky" and firms compete through differentiation and advertising instead. It is one illustration of interdependence, not the only model of oligopoly.

old:
Allocative: no — output is where MC = MR rather than AR = MC, so P > MC and there is a welfare loss to society. Productive: no — output is not at the lowest point of AC. X-inefficiency: possible — with little competition, costs may drift above their minimum.

Dynamic: yes — long-run supernormal profit gives both the means and the motive to invest in R&D, the monopolist's strongest defence.

old:
An industry with such a high proportion of fixed costs — water, rail, energy grids — that LRAC falls over the entire range of market demand: one firm can always supply the market more cheaply than several could.

The diagram shows the regulator's dilemma: a private profit-maximiser produces Qp at the high price Pp (grey guides), while pricing at P = MC (red guides, output Qn) is allocatively efficient but sets price below average cost, a loss needing subsidy.

old: Price discrimination is charging different consumers different prices for the same product, where the differences do not reflect costs. First-degree: each consumer pays the maximum they are willing to — auctions — capturing all consumer surplus. Second-degree: prices vary by quantity or version — bulk discounts, premium tiers. Third-degree: different consumer groups pay different prices by age, location or time of use — train tickets.
new:

old:
A contestable market is one with freedom of entry and exit. What disciplines firms is the threat of potential competition, not the number of firms currently in the market.

The distinction: competition is about how many firms there are; contestability is about how easily firms can enter and leave. A concentrated market can still behave competitively if it is highly contestable.

old:
Allocative: production where AR = MC — the optimal mix of goods for society. Productive: production at minimum AC, where MC = AC. Dynamic: long-run supernormal profits reinvested in R&D improve products and costs over time. X-inefficiency: without competitive pressure, costs drift above their minimum.

Static efficiency: resources both allocated and utilised in the most efficient way possible at a given point in time — requiring allocative and productive efficiency together.
new:
• Allocative: production where AR = MC — the optimal mix of goods for society.
  • Productive: production at minimum AC, where MC = AC.
  • Dynamic: long-run supernormal profits reinvested in R&D improve products and costs over time.
  • X-inefficiency: without competitive pressure, costs drift above their minimum.

Static efficiency: resources both allocated and utilised in the most efficient way possible at a given point in time — requiring allocative and productive efficiency together.

old:
The horizontal price line is tangent to the minimum of AC, and MC passes through the same point: P = MC gives allocative efficiency and minimum AC gives productive efficiency, both at the same output Q.

But with only normal profit there is nothing to reinvest, so dynamic efficiency is unlikely.
new:
The horizontal price line is tangent to the minimum of AC, and MC passes through the same point:

  • P = MC gives allocative efficiency.
  • Minimum AC gives productive efficiency.

Both sit at the same output Q.

But with only normal profit there is nothing to reinvest, so dynamic efficiency is unlikely.

old:
Profit-maximising at MC = MR, the firm stops short of both efficient points: P > MC, so there is allocative inefficiency — underproduction and a deadweight welfare loss — and output lies left of minimum AC, so there is productive inefficiency.

But P > AC means supernormal profit that can be reinvested in R&D — the potential for dynamic efficiency.
new:
Profit-maximising at MC = MR, the firm stops short of both efficient points:

  • P > MC, so there is allocative inefficiency — underproduction and a deadweight welfare loss.
  • Output lies left of minimum AC, so there is productive inefficiency.

But P > AC means supernormal profit that can be reinvested in R&D — the potential for dynamic efficiency.

old: Consumer surplus is the area below the demand curve and above the price line; producer surplus is the area above the supply curve and below the price line. Their sum is the social (community) surplus — total welfare — and it is maximised at the free-market equilibrium: any move away from it creates a welfare loss.
new:
• Consumer surplus is the area below the demand curve and above the price line.
  • Producer surplus is the area above the supply curve and below the price line.

Their sum is the social (community) surplus — total welfare — and it is maximised at the free-market equilibrium: any move away from it creates a welfare loss.

old:
MRP = MPP × MR. Marginal physical product (MPP): the extra output produced by one more worker. Marginal revenue (MR): the extra revenue gained from selling that extra output.

The MRP curve is the demand curve for labour, D(L), and it slopes downward because of the law of diminishing returns.
new:
MRP = MPP × MR

  • Marginal physical product (MPP): the extra output produced by one more worker.
  • Marginal revenue (MR): the extra revenue gained from selling that extra output.

The MRP curve is the demand curve for labour, D(L), and it slopes downward because of the law of diminishing returns.

old:
Supply of labour: the quantity of workers willing and able to work at a given wage rate. For a market or occupation the curve slopes upward — higher wages encourage more workers to enter the job.

Workers weigh monetary considerations — the wage, bonuses, overtime — against non-monetary considerations such as working conditions, flexible hours and other benefits.
new:
Supply of labour: the quantity of workers willing and able to work at a given wage rate. For a market or occupation the curve slopes upward — higher wages encourage more workers to enter the job.

Workers weigh:

  • Monetary considerations — the wage, bonuses, overtime.
  • Non-monetary considerations such as working conditions, flexible hours and other benefits.

old: A change in any factor other than the wage that affects willingness or ability to do the job: monetary benefits (stock options, bonuses, overtime pay), non-monetary benefits (working conditions, flexible hours, healthcare), demographic change and migration policy (the size of the available workforce), education and training (who is qualified to do it), and taxation and welfare benefits (the incentive to work at all).

  • Non-monetary benefits (working conditions, flexible hours, healthcare).
  • Demographic change and migration policy (the size of the available workforce).
  • Education and training (who is qualified to do it).
  • Taxation and welfare benefits (the incentive to work at all).

old:
Geographical immobility — workers cannot move easily to where the jobs are (high house prices and rent, expensive transport, lack of information). Occupational immobility — skills do not match the jobs available (few transferable skills, training and qualification requirements, technological change). Both cause structural unemployment and skill shortages.

Policies: education, training, apprenticeships and career guidance for occupational mobility; subsidised housing, relocation assistance, better transport and job information for geographical.
new:
• Geographical immobility — workers cannot move easily to where the jobs are (high house prices and rent, expensive transport, lack of information).

Both cause structural unemployment and skill shortages.

Policies: education, training, apprenticeships and career guidance for occupational mobility; subsidised housing, relocation assistance, better transport and job information for geographical.

old:
Three main causes: monopsony power (a single or dominant buyer of labour with wage-setting power), trade unions (workers' collective bargaining power, backed by the threat of industrial action) and imperfect information (workers do not know all wage rates and job opportunities, so make suboptimal employment decisions).

A monopsony is a single or dominant buyer of labour — the NHS in the UK healthcare labour market — able to pay workers less than their MRP.
new:
Three main causes:

  • Monopsony power (a single or dominant buyer of labour with wage-setting power).
  • Trade unions (workers' collective bargaining power, backed by the threat of industrial action).
  • Imperfect information (workers do not know all wage rates and job opportunities, so make suboptimal employment decisions).

A monopsony is a single or dominant buyer of labour — the NHS in the UK healthcare labour market — able to pay workers less than their MRP.

old:
The monopsonist faces the entire labour supply curve (S = AC): hiring one more worker means raising pay for existing workers too, so MCL lies above supply. It hires Qm, where MCL = MRP, and with wage-setting power pays only Wm — the lowest wage workers will accept, read off the supply curve.

Compared with the competitive outcome (Wc, Qc), a monopsony employs fewer workers at a lower wage.

old:
Depends on its size: far above equilibrium, it raises incomes significantly but creates substantial real wage unemployment. Depends on the wage elasticity of labour demand: with elastic demand the job losses are larger — the NMW works best where demand is wage inelastic.

And depends on motivation: if higher pay makes workers more productive, the rise in firms' average costs is offset and fewer jobs are lost.
new:
• Depends on its size: far above equilibrium, it raises incomes significantly but creates substantial real wage unemployment.
  • Depends on the wage elasticity of labour demand: with elastic demand the job losses are larger — the NMW works best where demand is wage inelastic.
  • And depends on motivation: if higher pay makes workers more productive, the rise in firms' average costs is offset and fewer jobs are lost.

old: Monopsony power — employers control the labour market enough to set wages below competitive levels. Information asymmetry — workers cannot see wage rates and opportunities, so cannot negotiate fair pay, and firms exploit this by offering some groups less. Bias and prejudice — employers hold discriminatory attitudes towards certain groups. Lack of regulation — insufficient legislation and enforcement lets discriminatory pay stand.
new:
• Monopsony power — employers control the labour market enough to set wages below competitive levels.
  • Information asymmetry — workers cannot see wage rates and opportunities, so cannot negotiate fair pay, and firms exploit this by offering some groups less.
  • Bias and prejudice — employers hold discriminatory attitudes towards certain groups.
  • Lack of regulation — insufficient legislation and enforcement lets discriminatory pay stand.

old:
The gender wage gap and the ethnic wage gap — differences in average earnings between men and women, and between ethnic groups.

Impacts: reduced income and living standards for discriminated workers; reduced employment and fewer opportunities to advance, entrenching inequality; and economic inefficiency — employers who do not hire the most qualified candidates misallocate resources, lowering productivity and growth.

old:
Education and skills — unequal access drives wage disparities. The tax system — progressive taxation redistributes towards lower incomes. Welfare payments — support the disposable income of the poorest. The minimum wage — lifts the lowest earners. Trade unions — negotiate better pay for low- and middle-income workers.

And the distribution of assets itself: who already holds property and financial investments shapes the income they generate.
new:
• Education and skills — unequal access drives wage disparities.
  • The tax system — progressive taxation redistributes towards lower incomes.
  • Welfare payments — support the disposable income of the poorest.
  • The minimum wage — lifts the lowest earners.
  • Trade unions — negotiate better pay for low- and middle-income workers.
  • The distribution of assets itself: who already holds property and financial investments shapes the income they generate.

old:
Equality: everyone receives an equal share of resources or opportunities — objective and measurable. Equity: everyone receives a "fair" share — subjective and open to debate, a value judgement.

What counts as equitable is contested: socialists favour a more equal distribution, capitalists a distribution based on merit and effort, and libertarians whatever free market forces produce with minimal intervention.
new:
• Equality: everyone receives an equal share of resources or opportunities — objective and measurable.
  • Equity: everyone receives a "fair" share — subjective and open to debate, a value judgement.

What counts as equitable is contested:

  • Socialists favour a more equal distribution.
  • Capitalists a distribution based on merit and effort.
  • Libertarians whatever free market forces produce with minimal intervention.

old:
Lower productivity — poor nutrition and healthcare limit output and LRAS growth. Lower tax revenue — low incomes shrink what the government can spend on infrastructure and services. Higher government spending — more needed on welfare and social services.

Loss of skills — those in poverty cannot develop their potential, weakening the workforce. And social unrest — crime and instability that deter investment and growth.
new:
• Lower productivity — poor nutrition and healthcare limit output and LRAS growth.
  • Lower tax revenue — low incomes shrink what the government can spend on infrastructure and services.
  • Higher government spending — more needed on welfare and social services.
  • Loss of skills — those in poverty cannot develop their potential, weakening the workforce.
  • Social unrest — crime and instability that deter investment and growth.

old:
Progressive direct taxes funding redistribution; welfare payments (unemployment, child and housing benefits); a minimum wage to floor the pay of low-paid workers; education and training to raise skills and employability.

Plus subsidies for essential goods — food, healthcare, housing — and free-at-use public services that cut the financial burden on low-income households.
new:
• Progressive direct taxes funding redistribution.
  • Welfare payments (unemployment, child and housing benefits).
  • A minimum wage to floor the pay of low-paid workers.
  • Education and training to raise skills and employability.
  • Subsidies for essential goods — food, healthcare, housing.
  • Free-at-use public services that cut the financial burden on low-income households.

old:
Unintended consequences: generous welfare can blunt the incentive to work; minimum wage rises can cost jobs or hours among the low-paid. Opportunity cost: redistribution is expensive, and the spending comes at the expense of other public services or investment.

And the equity–efficiency trade-off: progressive taxation redistributes, but may weaken incentives to work and invest, slowing the growth that funds redistribution in the first place.

old:
Non-excludability — it is impossible or extremely costly to prevent non-payers from consuming the good once it is provided. Non-rivalry — one person's consumption does not reduce the amount available for others.

Because non-payers cannot be excluded, everyone waits for someone else to pay — the free rider problem. With no way to charge, firms have no profit incentive and the good goes unprovided: complete market failure, which is why the state provides public goods through taxation. Technological change can shift the boundary — subscription streaming made television excludable.

  • Non-rivalry — one person's consumption does not reduce the amount available for others.

old:
Private costs and benefits fall on those directly in the transaction; external costs and benefits fall on third parties; social costs and benefits are the totals for society.

MSC = MPC + MEC and MSB = MPB + MEB. Externality diagrams are built from these identities: the gap between a private curve and its social twin is the externality.

• Private costs and benefits fall on those directly in the transaction.
  • External costs and benefits fall on third parties.
  • Social costs and benefits are the totals for society.

MSC = MPC + MEC and MSB = MPB + MEB.

Externality diagrams are built from these identities: the gap between a private curve and its social twin is the externality.

old:
Factor immobility — the inability of factors of production to move freely between different uses or locations, so resources are not put to their most productive use.

Geographical immobility — workers cannot move to areas with higher wages, due to housing costs or family commitments. Occupational immobility — workers cannot move between occupations for lack of skills or qualifications. Both cause shortages and surpluses of labour — a market failure.
new:
Factor immobility — the inability of factors of production to move freely between different uses or locations, so resources are not put to their most productive use.

  • Geographical immobility — workers cannot move to areas with higher wages, due to housing costs or family commitments.
  • Occupational immobility — workers cannot move between occupations for lack of skills or qualifications.

Both cause shortages and surpluses of labour — a market failure.

old:
Public ownership — ownership of enterprises by the government (nationalisation takes private firms into state hands), aiming to provide essential services and control natural monopolies. Privatisation — the transfer of ownership from the government to the private sector, aiming at efficiency, competition and a lighter fiscal burden.

On the natural-monopoly diagram, the state prices at the allocatively efficient point (AR = LRMC): lower price, higher output, more consumer surplus. A private owner profit-maximises (MR = MC): higher price, lower output, higher profit.
new:
• Public ownership — ownership of enterprises by the government (nationalisation takes private firms into state hands), aiming to provide essential services and control natural monopolies.
  • Privatisation — the transfer of ownership from the government to the private sector, aiming at efficiency, competition and a lighter fiscal burden.

On the natural-monopoly diagram:

  • The state prices at the allocatively efficient point (AR = LRMC): lower price, higher output, more consumer surplus.
  • A private owner profit-maximises (MR = MC): higher price, lower output, higher profit.

old:
To correct market failure, raise revenue, promote equity, and support firms — reflecting the government's range of objectives in a mixed economy.

The AQA toolkit: indirect taxation, subsidies, price controls (maximum and minimum prices), state provision, regulation, the extension of property rights and tradable pollution permits.

The toolkit:

  • Indirect taxation.
  • Subsidies.
  • Price controls (maximum and minimum prices).
  • State provision.
  • Regulation.
  • The extension of property rights and tradable pollution permits.

old: Explain AQA's other intervention methods: pollution permits, state provision and information provision.

State provision — direct supply of merit goods like education and healthcare, available regardless of ability to pay, at an opportunity cost. Information provision — campaigns shift D=MPB towards the social optimum, but only work if consumers respond.
